findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded install script
findings.whyItBreaks: Builds execute whatever content https://example.com/install.sh serves at build time. A compromised server, DNS/TLS supply-chain failure, or changed script can silently run arbitrary commands in the image build.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build downloads and runs whatever `https://example.com/install.sh` serves at that moment. A compromised origin, DNS/TLS trust failure, or changed script can execute arbitrary code in the build and silently alter the resulting image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: This pipes a remotely hosted, unpinned script directly into a root shell during every image build. A changed or compromised response at the URL compromises the produced image, and builds are not reproducible.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported helper discards that error and returns "", the same result as a present key whose value is empty. Callers cannot reliably distinguish absence from a legitimate value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the public API
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing and returns "" for both an absent key and a present key with an empty value. As an exported API, callers cannot distinguish failure from valid stored data and may treat missing data as real.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in the public helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but LoadOrDefault discards it and returns "", which is also a valid stored map value. Its public API therefore forces callers to treat a failed lookup as a successful empty value.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each result write is detached into a goroutine, so Run can return before any result is delivered. A caller that closes the results channel or proceeds assuming all jobs are complete immediately after Run returns can cause send-on-closed-channel panics or observe incomplete results. Previously, Run returned only after every send completed.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every job result had been sent. The new goroutines outlive Run, so a caller that closes results immediately after Run returns will race with them and can panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot know when all results are available.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send is now detached in a goroutine, so Run can return while workers still send to results. A caller that used Run's previous completion behavior to close results immediately after it returns will cause those goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot reliably know when all results have been produced.

findings.title: Require admin status and matching tenant to delete
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `&&` to `||` makes `canDeleteRecord` return true for any non-admin whose tenant matches the record, allowing ordinary tenant users to delete records. It also allows an admin from a different tenant to delete the record. Both cases bypass the former tenant-scoped administrator authorization requirement.

findings.title: Require administrator status for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: For a session with isAdmin=false and tenantId equal to the record tenantId, this now returns true. Any ordinary user in a tenant can therefore pass the exported delete authorization check, whereas the previous policy required both tenant match and administrator status.

findings.title: Require admin and tenant match before deleting records
findings.whyItBreaks: With `||`, a session where `isAdmin=false` and `session.tenantId === record.tenantId` now receives delete permission. The prior policy required both conditions, so this is an authorization bypass; it also lets an admin delete a record from another tenant.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before saving settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts JSON and validation failures into valid defaults. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and calls save; for example, raw {"theme":"dark"} with size 18 now saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":18}, whereas it previously threw and performed no write. This silently discards the user's stored theme.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Any malformed or schema-invalid stored value now returns a normal Settings object. updateFontSize then changes its font size and saves it, replacing the original data with the default light theme rather than surfacing the parse failure and avoiding the write.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before saving settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch conflates malformed or schema-invalid input with valid default settings. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and saves it, overwriting the invalid stored value; previously JSON.parse or validation errors stopped the write and reached the caller.

findings.title: Keep report artifacts tied to the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom reports build.ref(branch) while artifacts are loaded from build.ref("verified"). The resulting report falsely associates verified artifacts with the requested branch commit.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom identifies the branch commit while artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. Consumers receive an internally inconsistent report.

findings.title: Use the requested commit when retrieving report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: When `branch` resolves to a different commit than `verified`, `builtFrom` reports the branch commit but `artifacts` belong to the verified commit. Consumers therefore receive a self-contradictory BuildReport and may publish or act on artifacts from the wrong build.

findings.title: Apply limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9, then writes every returned item, so feeds longer than 20 produce output longer than the intended page size.

findings.title: Respect limit when returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry rather than at most limit. renderFeed passes 20, then writes every returned entry into its output array, expanding the returned feed beyond 20 entries.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For limit=20, the function now returns every reversed entry rather than at most 20. renderFeed calls it with 20 at src/feed.ts:9, then copies every returned entry into its output, so feeds longer than 20 are no longer capped.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, this emits fewer data rows but retains `entries.length` in `# entry-count`. For example, one live and one stale entry produces `# entry-count: 2` followed by one row, violating the manifest's count contract.

findings.title: Pass live.length to the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is omitted but the unchanged header still receives entries.length. For example, one stale entry produces '# entry-count: 1' with zero manifest rows, so consumers relying on the declared count receive invalid metadata.

findings.title: Count only rendered entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: With any stale entry, the body emits only live rows but headerLines still receives entries.length. For example, one live and one stale entry produces '# entry-count: 2' followed by one entry row, so consumers trusting the header receive inconsistent manifest data.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter

findings.title: Preserve the orders-module shippingQuote export

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: The base revision exports shippingQuote from src/orders.ts, but the new revision exports only orderTotal. Any existing consumer importing shippingQuote from this module will fail to compile or receive an undefined named export at runtime after upgrading.

findings.title: Restore the exported shippingQuote compatibility API
findings.whyItBreaks: Consumers importing shippingQuote from src/orders can no longer compile (or resolve the named export at runtime). The replacement quoteShipping is exported only from a new module, so this is a breaking upgrade for the existing public entry point.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` uses `canProceed`; a draft with `payment: "missing"`, previously saved, now returns `"blocked"`. Payment may govern submission, but it does not legitimately govern saving an unfinished draft.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: For `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, this now returns false, so `saveDraft` returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Payment legitimately governs submission, but not persisting a draft.

findings.title: Keep payment independent of saving a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: The shared canProceed predicate now returns false for { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }. submitOrder legitimately requires payment, but saveDraft also consumes this predicate and returns "blocked", preventing users from saving an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Read files from the selected channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit is repo.headCommit(channel) but Snapshot.files comes from repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). Consumers will publish or inspect content that does not match the commit and channel advertised by the snapshot.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot reports `commit: head` for the requested `channel`, but its `files` are loaded from the unrelated `stable` ref. When the requested channel and stable differ, consumers receive internally inconsistent snapshots and may publish stable's files as the requested channel's commit.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: The returned snapshot reports `commit` as the requested channel's head, but populates `files` from the unrelated `stable` head. Publishing a non-stable channel therefore produces internally inconsistent snapshots and can publish stale/wrong files.

findings.title: Honor the advertised limit parameter

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int

findings.title: Use fromRevision to compute changed paths

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds

findings.title: Remove the stale retry milliseconds multiplier

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds

The first failed retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) rather than one second; later retries are likewise 1,000× too slow.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. Previously, Save returned f.Close()'s error after a successful flush; callers of this exported function can now receive nil even though finalizing the output file failed.

findings.title: Include each page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds return end as the first excluded index, but range(start, end - 1) excludes both end and end - 1. Every nonempty page loses its last row; a page_size of 1 produces no rows at all, so render_page and summarize silently omit data.

findings.title: Preserve public keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: All non-private functions rename their parameters (for example, page_window(page, size) becomes page_window(page_index, page_size)). Existing Python callers using documented/introspected keyword arguments, such as page_window(rows, page=0, size=25), now fail with TypeError before pagination runs.

findings.title: Include the page end index in page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds returned by _window_bounds define end as exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) also excludes the final valid index. Consequently, a one-row page renders empty and every larger page drops its last row; summarize therefore loses one row per page.

findings.title: Include the page end row
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds helper returns a half-open [start, end) interval, but range(start, end - 1) excludes end - 1. Consequently page_window, render_page, and summarize silently drop each page's last row; a one-row page renders empty.

findings.title: Return entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age below ttlMs, so get deletes it and returns null. Once its age exceeds ttlMs, get instead returns the stale entry indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating forward through jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item left while forEach advances its index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job is skipped and remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return entries only while they are within the TTL
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so for a normal positive TTL the `>` check is false and `get` deletes it as a miss. Once the entry is older than the TTL, the condition becomes true and it is returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating with forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into the current index, but `forEach` then advances to the next index. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job is skipped and remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return cache entries while they are still within the TTL
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so it fails `age > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs with forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into the current index, but `forEach` advances to the following index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve zero for an empty row set
findings.whyItBreaks: For [], reduce produces 0 and division by rows.length produces NaN. The prior behavior returned 0, so callers now receive an invalid aggregate value.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort` mutates `rows`. Previously `busiest` sorted a copy, so callers could safely retain their original order; this change silently reorders their input.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input result
findings.whyItBreaks: With rows=[], reduce returns 0 and division by rows.length returns NaN. Previously this public function returned 0 for the same valid empty-array input.

findings.title: Avoid mutating callers' row array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates `rows` in place. Calling busiest() now silently reorders the caller's data, whereas the prior implementation sorted a defensive copy.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the prior 0 result.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. Previously busiest sorted a copy, so callers could safely reuse their input order after requesting the busiest row.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before deriving cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numeric scores as strings. For players scored [8, 100, 9] with n=2, rankScores returns [9, 8, 100], making the cutoff 8; topPlayers then returns the first two input players ([8, 100]) rather than the actual top two ([100, 9]).

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers by their string representations. For scores [2, 11, 10] and n=2, rankScores produces [2, 11, 10], making the cutoff 11; topPlayers then returns only the player with 11 and drops the player with 10, despite 10 being the second-highest score.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score sort
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numeric scores as strings. For players [{score: 9}, {score: 100}] and n=1, rankScores returns [9, 100], so cutoff is 9 and topPlayers returns the first input player (score 9) instead of the score-100 player.

findings.title: Use a constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain string equality can stop at the first differing character, exposing comparison timing to an attacker who can repeatedly submit signature guesses. The previous hmac.compare_digest call avoided this timing oracle; handle() uses this result to authorize processor(payload).

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using string equality can return after the first differing character, exposing comparison-time differences to a remote caller. The prior hmac.compare_digest call was specifically designed to prevent leaking how much of the HMAC matched; handle() uses this result to authorize processor(payload).

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can return after the first differing character, exposing a timing oracle for the HMAC value. An attacker able to measure verification timing can incrementally infer a valid signature and submit an unauthorized webhook.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction ends after the ledger insert at line 23. If either balance UPDATE at line 24 fails, the ledger entry has already committed; a failure after the debit can also leave balances partially updated. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep all transfer writes in the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits at line 23, then both balance updates run outside it. If either update fails, the prior ledger entry cannot roll back; if the credit update fails after the debit succeeds, balances are also left inconsistent. Previously all three writes were atomic.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction now commits immediately after the ledger insert. If either balance update fails, the ledger records a completed transfer while balances are unchanged or only the debit is applied. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing dates
findings.whyItBreaks: This changes the established UTC billing-day contract to the server's local timezone. For example, an instant at 2026-01-02T00:30:00Z becomes 2026-01-01 on a UTC-08 host, so the same event can be assigned to different billing days depending on deployment timezone; sameBillingDay inherits that changed classification.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly derived all components with UTC getters. The new local-time getters make the result environment-dependent: for example, in America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now produces 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-01. This also changes sameBillingDay outcomes around UTC midnight.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: This changes the established UTC billing-day contract to depend on the server's timezone. For example, at 2026-09-16T20:00:00Z, a UTC+08 host now returns 2026-09-17 while the previous implementation returned 2026-09-16. The same instant can therefore be assigned to different billing days across deployments.

findings.title: Include the tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a successful read for ('tenant-a', 'acct-1'), a read for ('tenant-b', 'acct-1') uses the same key and returns the cached tenant-a Profile at line 16 without calling fetchProfile. This misroutes tenant-scoped profile data.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account X, a read for tenant B and account X returns A’s cached Profile without calling fetchProfile. This exposes incorrect cross-tenant profile data and leaves the returned Profile.tenant inconsistent with the requested tenant.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants using the same account ID now share one memo entry. After tenant A caches account X, a request for tenant B/account X returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `missing: <key>`; it now returns `""`, which is also a valid `Map<string, string>` value. Callers, including `loadAll`, can no longer distinguish absent data from a deliberately stored empty string.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing map entry previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a stored empty value. `loadAll` therefore returns partial-looking successful results instead of reporting a missing required key.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw, but now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a key explicitly stored with an empty value. loadAll consequently returns partial-looking successful data instead of reporting the missing key.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing Config callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers supplying the previously required `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because both `timeout` and `retries` are newly required. JavaScript callers retain no deadline: `config.timeout` is undefined, so `Date.now() > deadline` is always false and retry performs all attempts despite the former timeout.

findings.title: Expose failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: When every invocation of `fn` throws, this exported function catches every exception and returns void exactly as it does after a successful invocation. Public callers therefore cannot distinguish exhausted retries from success and can act on failed work as though it completed.

findings.title: Expose failure when background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from `fn` is discarded and, after the retry budget is exhausted, this exported function returns `undefined`—the same observable result as a successful invocation. Callers cannot distinguish a completed retry from a failed one and may treat failed work as complete.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using the exported `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` Config can no longer compile because `timeoutMs` was removed and unrelated `retries` is now required. Untyped existing callers instead pass `timeout: undefined`; `Date.now() + undefined` becomes NaN, so the deadline check never stops retries.

findings.title: Propagate exhausted background retry failures
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` is exported but catches every exception and returns `void` after all retries fail. Its caller therefore cannot distinguish a successful invocation from one where every invocation of `fn` failed, making failed background work appear successful.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop contract now permits a number, but numbers have no `length`. For example, `value={42}` renders `len=undefined` rather than a meaningful value-derived label, so the new public input type is not implemented correctly.

findings.title: Support numeric Field values when computing the label
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now promises `number` is accepted, but `number` has no `length` property. TypeScript rejects this expression; if emitted without type checking, `<Field value={42}>` renders `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed public prop type permits number, but number has no length property. TypeScript reports an error for value.length; if emitted despite type errors, a numeric value renders as "len=undefined".

score.error: critic produced no summary or checked list (likely malformed output)

findings.title: Retain the diff output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `git()` now uses Node's default 1 MiB `maxBuffer`, but it is used to capture the complete patch at line 140. A PR with more than 1 MiB of textual diff output causes `spawnSync` to terminate/truncate the git process and this helper throws, so Needlefish posts a failed check instead of reviewing it. The prior implementation explicitly supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore the diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Node's default spawnSync maxBuffer is 1 MiB. The git helper reads the full `git diff` output at line 140, so a PR whose patch exceeds that size causes spawnSync to terminate with a buffer error; runGithub then fails the review instead of producing a result.

findings.title: Restore a sufficient buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: `runGithub` obtains the full PR patch through this wrapper at line 140. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses its 1 MiB default; a PR diff exceeding that size causes the git process result to fail, the wrapper throws, and the review is replaced by a failed check rather than reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes `codex exec` use its configured sandbox policy. A host configured for `workspace-write` or a more permissive mode can now write to `opts.repoPath` while processing a review prompt, whereas the prior invocation prevented writes. This allows a review run to alter the checkout it is meant only to inspect.

findings.title: Restore the read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` lets the invoked Codex CLI use its configured sandbox policy instead of enforcing review-only access. A review of an untrusted repository can then execute modifying commands or alter the repository, violating the review agent's safety boundary.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` leaves `codex exec` to use its configured/default workspace-write permission profile. Since this exported wrapper runs arbitrary review prompts with `cwd` set to `opts.repoPath`, a prompt-injection instruction from repository content can now cause Codex to alter files in the worktree rather than being enforced as a non-mutating reviewer.

findings.title: Restore merge-base comparison for PR base refs
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA may be a newer commit on the PR's base branch than the branch point. When it contains commits absent from HEAD, `git diff baseSha HEAD` produces inverse changes for those base-only commits, so the review bundle and inline-comment path set include files not changed by the PR.

findings.title: Build the review diff from the configured PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_HEAD_SHA is still read as the PR commit and used when posting the review/check, but the patch and changed-file list are now computed against HEAD. When Actions checks out a merge ref or another revision, Needlefish reviews that checkout while attaching its result to PR_HEAD_SHA, so findings can describe files/lines not present in the reviewed PR commit.

findings.title: Restore the merge-base/PR-head diff range
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch tip and the PR branch is behind it, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes target-only changes as removals, so unrelated files enter the review bundle. It also ignores the supplied PR_HEAD_SHA while reviews are posted against that SHA, allowing the analyzed checkout to differ from the reviewed commit.

findings.title: Preserve dollar signs when embedding prompt data
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement value. bundle.patch is arbitrary diff text and may contain these tokens; candidate fields may as well. For example, a patch containing $& is injected into critic.md as the matched {{PATCH}} marker rather than literal $&, so runCodex receives a corrupted review prompt and can review different source content.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets replacement-string tokens such as $&, $`, $', and $$. A reviewed patch containing a normal source literal such as "$&" is expanded while replacing {{PATCH}}, inserting the placeholder itself instead of the literal patch text; $` and $' can duplicate surrounding critic-prompt content. The same corruption applies to serialized bundle and findings data, so Codex can receive malformed or incomplete review context.

findings.title: Use callback replacements to preserve literal reviewer input
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace with a string replacement expands $&, $`, $', and $$ sequences. A reviewed patch or generated finding containing (for example) "$&" is changed into the placeholder text rather than delivered literally to the review/critic prompt; "$`" and "$'" additionally inject portions of the prompt template. This causes Codex to review corrupted input.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review POST fails, this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults it to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR advances after headSha was captured but before this fallback runs, Needlefish posts an approval or change request for newer, unreviewed code rather than the commit used to build the result.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review bound to the analyzed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The initial request is explicitly built from headSha, which is the SHA diffed and reviewed. If that request fails and a new commit is pushed before the fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub create the fallback review on the PR's then-most-recent commit instead. The review verdict therefore appears to cover code that Needlefish never analyzed.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed findings no longer produce the validation error previously exposed by this public normalizer. For example, an omitted file and lineStart now become file="" and lineStart=0 while being returned as a Finding; invalid severity/category are similarly recast as P1/bug. Callers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a real, actionable finding.

findings.title: Keep the exported strict mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the public strict parameter breaks TypeScript callers of normalizeReview(raw, false). JavaScript callers still pass the extra argument, but their requested lenient behavior has changed from dropping malformed entries to returning fabricated P1 findings.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-finding failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or incomplete finding records that previously caused normalization to fail now become a P1/bug finding with an empty file, line 0, and empty rationale fields. Callers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a real finding and may render or persist invalid review data.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of coercing them into P1 bugs
findings.whyItBreaks: An input such as `{ severity: "P9", lineStart: 0 }` previously raised a malformed-output error. It now becomes a seemingly valid P1/bug finding with an empty file and line 0, so every consumer of this exported normalizer must conflate invalid review JSON with a real blocking finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers of `normalizeReview(raw, false)` no longer type-check, and JavaScript callers silently get different behavior: malformed findings that were filtered in lenient mode are now emitted as fabricated default findings.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before any checkout (the first checkout is line 42). `gh pr view <number>` resolves its repository from a local repository unless `-R` or `GH_REPO` is supplied; the removed REPO/-R context therefore makes manual dispatch fail in a clean runner, or use stale self-hosted workspace context.

findings.title: Retain explicit repository selection for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, this step runs before the checkout at line 42, so `gh pr view` has no checked-out repository remote from which to infer a target. Removing `-R "$REPO"` makes resolving the supplied PR number fail (or depend on stale self-hosted-runner state), preventing the manual review workflow from running.

findings.title: Keep the target repository when resolving manually dispatched PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, this step runs before actions/checkout, so there is no checked-out repository from which gh can infer a target. The workflow no longer supplies --repo or GH_REPO; gh pr view therefore cannot determine which repository owns PR_NUM and the ref-resolution step fails, preventing the advertised manual review workflow from running.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or wrongly typed required review fields previously threw a malformed-output error, but now become empty strings and arrays. Because normalizeReview is exported, callers can no longer distinguish an invalid/truncated review response from a legitimate review with no findings or residual risks.

findings.title: Preserve malformed review rejection
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or incorrectly typed top-level review fields previously threw a malformed-output error. They now become an empty summary, findings, checked list, and residual risks, which is indistinguishable from a legitimate empty review. As an exported function, this forces callers to treat invalid model/parser output as a successful review.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, a missing or wrongly typed required field threw a malformed-review error. This path now substitutes empty strings and arrays, so invalid reviewer output is indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings or residual risks. As an exported function, this public contract forces callers to treat a failed parse as a valid result.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The new checkout expression therefore falls back to github.ref instead of the input PR's head, BASE_REF falls back to main, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty. A manually entered PR number can consequently be reviewed using the dispatcher-selected branch's source and no resolved PR SHAs, whereas the removed step queried that PR's head/base refs.

findings.title: Resolve refs for manually dispatched PR reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, the pull_request event object does not exist, so both expressions evaluate empty. The required pr_number is still passed to the CLI, but PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are no longer populated from that PR. The checkout at line 29 likewise falls back to github.ref rather than the selected PR head, causing a manual run to inspect the workflow branch instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR head for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch events have no pull_request payload, so this expression falls back to github.ref: the branch from which the workflow was manually launched, not the head SHA of inputs.pr_number. Dispatching from main to review an open PR therefore installs and runs main's Needlefish source instead of that PR's revision. The same missing payload also leaves PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA empty at lines 45-46.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for generated diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal obtains the entire patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]). With spawnSync's default 1 MiB maxBuffer, a diff exceeding that size is terminated and git() throws before review() receives the bundle. The previous implementation explicitly supported outputs up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore the git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. runLocal reads the entire patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at line 100, so any review diff larger than 1 MiB now terminates git with an output-buffer error and aborts the local review instead of sending the patch to review().

findings.title: Preserve the git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal reads the complete git diff into stdout. Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default; reviewing a repository diff larger than that fails before the bundle is constructed, whereas the prior code supported diffs up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Report review execution failures as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or posting results throws, the exception path now creates a completed Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub accepts neutral as satisfying a required status check, so a PR can merge even though Needlefish did not produce a review. The prior implementation emitted "failure".

findings.title: Report review failures as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, the code still records the error text but publishes the Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats neutral as a successful required status, so a branch rule requiring this check can permit merging even though the review failed and the summary explicitly says it did not pass.

findings.title: Keep review failures failing
findings.whyItBreaks: When review execution or result posting throws, the adapter now posts Needlefish with conclusion "neutral" despite stating the PR did not pass. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check status, so a branch rule requiring Needlefish can permit merge without a completed review.

findings.title: Restore a trusted checkout for the reviewer executable
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is checked out at lines 43-47, then its src/cli.ts is executed here. A same-repository PR can modify the reviewer (or its dependency/install inputs) so arbitrary PR-controlled code runs on the self-hosted runner with GH_TOKEN, which has pull-request and checks write permissions.

findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is now the installation and execution directory. A same-repository PR can alter package lifecycle scripts, dependencies, or src/cli.ts; those changes execute on the self-hosted runner with GH_TOKEN holding pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. The prior workflow deliberately checked out the tool from trusted main to prevent this.

findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json at the reviewed SHA; it has no package.json, pnpm lockfile, node_modules/.bin/tsx, or src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install --frozen-lockfile fails before review, and the CLI path would also be absent.

The workflow installs and executes those PR-controlled files on a self-hosted runner while GH_TOKEN has pull-requests:write and checks:write, allowing a malicious PR to forge review output, alter PR state, or compromise the runner.

findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install has no project manifest and the final command cannot locate either ./node_modules/.bin/tsx or src/cli.ts, so every review job fails before reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Normalize severity input before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external review JSON, but a valid severity serialized as " p0 " or "p0" now fails the exact-membership check and is returned as P3. This silently downgrades the finding instead of preserving its intended severity.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` accepts untyped parsed output and passes each item to this function. A finding such as `{ "severity": "p0" }` or `{ "severity": " P1 " }`, which previously normalized to P0/P1, now fails the exact-match check and is reported as P3. This can incorrectly downgrade real review findings.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization and P1 fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs previously accepted by the normalizer, such as "p1", " P1 ", or a missing severity, now become P3. normalizeReview passes untyped parsed findings through this function, so equivalent review output is silently returned with a lower severity.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex child environment
findings.whyItBreaks: With no `env` option, `spawnSync` inherits `process.env`, so `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN` become available to the Codex process. The removed code explicitly prevented this; a prompted or compromised Codex subprocess can now read and use repository-owner GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env option, spawnSync inherits process.env. This passes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN into the Codex process while it analyzes a caller-selected repository and prompt. Repository/prompt-controlled agent instructions can cause those credentials to be read and exposed, defeating the prior credential boundary.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit `env`, `spawnSync` inherits `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. This wrapper executes the binary selected by the externally configurable `CODEX_BIN` and supplies it a prompt while it operates in a repository; the prior allowlist-by-deletion prevented that child process from reading GitHub credentials. The read-only sandbox argument restricts filesystem writes, not environment-secret access.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach this self-hosted job, which checks out the fork's head SHA and executes its dependency-install and CLI commands. A fork author can therefore run arbitrary code on the runner and potentially compromise persistent runner state or data available to later jobs.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running on self-hosted runners
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now trigger this self-hosted job, which checks out the fork-controlled head SHA (lines 20-24) and executes its dependency installation and CLI (lines 28 and 34). A fork author can alter package metadata or source to execute arbitrary commands on the runner and access its host-level credentials or persistent state.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach this self-hosted job, which checks out attacker-controlled commits, runs their dependency install scripts, and executes their TypeScript. A fork author can therefore execute arbitrary code on the persistent runner and access any runner-local credentials or state.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously valid input "0" returned 0. It now returns fallbackMs, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 waits 5000ms before SIGKILL and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000ms before resolving, instead of honoring the configured immediate transition.

findings.title: Restore deep-review coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapped hotspots are now deep-reviewed. A changed file omitted by the mapper, or assigned only to a hotspot after that limit, is never reviewed and is not surfaced as a blocking residual risk, so a large PR can receive a clean result while containing an unchecked change.

findings.title: Propagate residual risks from successful deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Residual risks reported by successful deep passes are discarded and replaced with an empty array before the critic receives the candidate. The critic can no longer distinguish a review with blockers from one without them, allowing a blocked condition to be omitted from the final verdict.

findings.title: Keep the failure rationale in the finding deduplication key
findings.whyItBreaks: Distinct findings at the same location and category with titles sharing their first 60 normalized characters now collide even when they describe different breakages. The lower-severity finding is silently dropped, whereas the previous key retained distinct rationale.

findings.title: Forward deep-review residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep pass can return a blocking residual risk when it cannot verify material behavior. This now replaces every such signal with [], so the critic and final deriveVerdict call cannot distinguish an incomplete deep review from a clean one and can return PASS.

findings.title: Deep-review files omitted by the top six hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews select at most six hotspots, but the removed tail-coverage pass was the only mechanism that added changed files absent from those hotspots. A mapper result with seven separate surfaces, or one that omits a file, now leaves those changed files without any deep review; the final critic receives only patchStat for large reviews and cannot recover the omitted diff analysis.

findings.title: Convert failed deep passes into blocking review results
findings.whyItBreaks: A transient runCodex, JSON extraction, or normalization failure for one hotspot now escapes reviewLarge and aborts the entire review. Previously that same failure produced a blocking residual risk and preserved results from the remaining hotspots.

findings.title: Preserve focus when constructing large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For bundles routed to reviewLarge, focus is no longer included in the map prompt and is no longer substituted into each deep-review prompt. A caller requesting review of a specific area therefore receives an unfocused large-PR review, while the small-review path still forwards the complete bundle.

findings.title: Preserve focus when constructing large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path previously substituted bundle.focus into every deep-review prompt. After this change, callers can still supply focus but it is never forwarded to either the map or deep pass, so a requested review area is silently ignored for large patches while it remains part of the input bundle.

findings.title: Preserve focus for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When a bundle exceeds the large-review threshold, review() selects reviewLarge(), but this change removes focus from both the map bundle and every deep-review prompt. A caller-supplied focus is therefore honored for small reviews (which serialize the full bundle) but ignored for large reviews, the path where directed review is most important.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations from 119500ms through 119999ms, minutes is computed as 1 while seconds rounds to 60, so rendered review stats report "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". Likewise, 59500ms renders as "60s" rather than "1m 0s".

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, this computes minutes=1 and seconds=60, so rendered review statistics show "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". The same boundary causes 59500ms to display as "60s" rather than rolling over.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations from 59,500ms through 59,999ms, `seconds` rounds to 60 while `minutes` remains 0, producing `60s` instead of the prior `1m 0s`. From 119,500ms through 119,999ms it produces `1m 60s`; this formatting reaches the rendered review stats and total duration.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger` promises positive values in both its exported name and error contract, but the changed `< 0` guard returns `0` successfully. Public callers can therefore receive a value that violates the stated positive-integer guarantee.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger now returns 0 even though its exported name and error contract require a positive integer. Consumers relying on this parser for values such as timeouts or attempt counts can receive an invalid zero value instead of a validation error.

findings.title: Reject zero as a non-positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger and its error text promise a positive integer, but input "0" now passes the guard and returns 0. Public callers can therefore receive a value outside the validator's stated contract.
